newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: RESEARCH ALERT - Downgrade Malaysia, says Sassoon.
newsitem.headline: RESEARCH ALERT - Downgrade Malaysia, says Sassoon.

text.p: Research firm J.M.Sassoon & Co on Friday advised investors in a research report to downgrade Malaysia and upgrade Singapore in the short- and medium-term.

"We would like to revise our market view. With an eye on short and medium-term relative performance, we would advise downgrading Malaysia and upgrading Singapore," analyst Lim Eng Hai said in Sassoon's Singapore/Malaysia Market Outlook & Strategy.
He said Malaysia was earlier expected to outperform Singapore at least in the first half of 1997.
"However, the big picture is changing before our eyes and a lot sooner than expected," the report said.
Lim said the primary reason for the revision was the Malaysian central bank, Bank Negara's imposition of lending curbs to the property sector and for purchase of stocks.
Bank Negara announced last week that effective April 1 bank loans to the property sector should not exceed 20 percent of their total outstanding loans.
The 15 percent of total loans limit on lending against shares and units of unit trusts as collateral was also extended to include buying of stocks.
The key Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index has fallen about 7.5 percent this week, mainly in reaction to the Bank Negara lending curbs. The fall was led by property and banking stocks.

Lim said after laying to rest concerns about overheating in the economy and growing current account imbalances last year, Malaysia was "well positioned to profit from a time of plenty with countless infrastructure projects".
"In contrast, Singapore was struggling with a very soft export sector and heading for a possible correction in the residential property market," he said.
He said the Bank Negara move was good for the economy in the long-term.

"But, in the short to medium-term (roughly the next six to nine months), the Bank Negara actions will be very negative on for major sectors of the economy such as property and banking," Lim said in the report.
